t: The three typefaces this site is set in
d: One for the interface, one for reading and one for the name: the type behind Creators Lab.
x: Creators Lab is set in three typefaces, and each has one job. DM Mono, for almost everything Every label, headline and button on this site is DM Mono, a monospaced family in three weights and three styles designed by Colophon Foundry for DeepMind, with creative direction from the DeepMind team. It is loosely based on DM Sans, with lower contrast, and was added to Google Fonts in April 2020. A monospace makes everything look like a record of something: a lab note, a set time, a catalogue number. That is the mood we wanted. Newsreader, for reading Long articles switch to Newsreader, a serif commissioned by Google Fonts and designed by Hugues Gentile with art direction by Jean-Baptiste Levée at Production Type. It was made for continuous reading on screens, and it comes in optical sizes, so the letters change shape slightly between caption size and display size. It joined Google Fonts in July 2020. Archivo, for the name The CREATORS LAB wordmark is Archivo at its widest and heaviest. Archivo is a grotesque sans by Héctor Gatti and the Omnibus-Type team, originally designed for highlights and headlines and built to work in print and on screen at the same time. We use it nowhere else. Why three One voice for the interface, one for reading and one for the name keeps the site calm. The only colour we add is a single electric blue, #2723F1. Everything else is black, white and grey.

d: How a tool for making stem cells became longevity science’s biggest bet, what it has shown so far, and what could go wrong.
x: Partial reprogramming is an attempt to make old cells behave like young ones without turning them into something else. It borrows a tool from stem cell biology and uses it gently. Where it comes from In 2006 Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka showed that four genes, Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc, could turn adult mouse fibroblasts into induced pluripotent stem cells: cells that can become almost any tissue. Full reprogramming like this erases what a cell is. Partial reprogramming tries to stop well before that point. What it is meant to reset Cells carry a layer of chemical marks on their DNA, the epigenome, which helps decide which genes are read. Those marks change with age in ways regular enough to measure. In 2013 Steve Horvath built an epigenetic clock from DNA methylation at 353 sites, trained on about 8,000 samples from 51 tissues and cell types. Reprogramming winds that kind of clock back. The open question is whether winding it back makes tissue work better. The evidence so far In 2016 a team led by Juan Carlos Izpisua Belmonte switched the four factors on in short cycles in mice that age prematurely. The mice showed fewer signs of ageing and lived longer. In 2020 David Sinclair's lab at Harvard used three of the factors, leaving out c-Myc, to reverse vision loss in a mouse model of glaucoma and in old mice. In 2026 the idea reached people. Life Biosciences began a first-in-human safety trial of ER-100, which delivers those three genes into one eye of patients with glaucoma or NAION. We covered the trial in Rewinding the Cell. The money Altos Labs launched in January 2022 with $3 billion committed, one of the largest raises in biotech, and with Yamanaka as an unpaid senior scientific adviser. Retro Biosciences began with $180 million from Sam Altman and works on reprogramming alongside other approaches, and in May 2026 it announced the first close of a new round at a $1.8 billion valuation. What could go wrong The same factors that rejuvenate can also erase identity, and cells that forget what they are can form tumours. That is why most groups switch the factors on briefly, use fewer of them, or look for drugs that do part of the job. No partial reprogramming treatment has yet been proven to work in people.

t: The Creators Lab 01 cover, in detail
d: Four floating islands, a guitarist, a reader and a creature with a mug: a closer look at Joe Taylor’s cover for our first issue.
x: The cover of Creators Lab 01 is by Joe Taylor, the Berlin-based British illustrator and animator. It is a single scene, drawn in his usual thick, even line and flat colour, and it rewards a slow look. Read it from the top The sky fades from lavender at the top to peach and then pale yellow near the ground, like the last ten minutes of a summer evening. Four islands float in it, each with a flat green top and a jagged underside, as if they had been pulled out of the ground like teeth. On the smallest island, near the centre, a tiny figure lies back and reads. To the right, a larger island sprouts long green plants that curl over its edges like tentacles. Lower down, a red-haired figure in a lavender jumper sits on a rock and plays an acoustic guitar, eyes closed. In the foreground, a lavender creature with a long nose and two thin antennae holds a mug in a yellow hand, surrounded by soft green plants. It looks perfectly at home. Why it is the first cover Creators Lab is about people who make things: in a lab, in a studio, behind a pair of turntables. Joe's scene has all three moods in it: someone studying, someone playing, someone simply watching with a warm drink. His animated work, for clients including Apple, Netflix and TED-Ed, rarely sits still. On paper, he gave us a world that does, for a moment. Read our profile of the artist: Joe Taylor's soft, strange worlds.

d: The Berlin animator and illustrator whose soft, strange worlds never quite sit still.
x: Joe Taylor draws the kind of creatures you half remember from a dream: soft-edged, slightly lopsided, cheerfully strange. A British animator and illustrator based in Berlin, he started out as a graphic designer before illustration and animation took over. Much of his work moves. His illustrations loop and morph, so his portfolio never quite sits still. That style has carried him to clients including Apple, Netflix and TED-Ed, and onto Vinyl Moon record jackets, including a gatefold for Space Case with a rotating artwork spinner. He also makes music as J Yerolota, which might explain why so much of his work feels like it has a groove underneath it. With fellow animator Alex Gamsu Jenkins, he made the 2022 video for "For Willow" by the Berlin house producer Moomin. It opens on a barren landscape that slowly comes back to life, greenery creeping over everything until the whole world is lush and strange. For Creators Lab, Joe made the artwork for our first print issue: calm creatures, floating gardens, a cup of something warm. It is a gentle world, and a good one to spend time in.

t: Detroit Dust on a Melbourne Floor
d: Fourteen years after a rare 2012 visit, the Detroit house icon returns for CORE Melbourne and a Sunday session at the Forum.
x: There's a hush that falls over a Moodymann crowd in the first ten minutes. It isn't boredom. It's a room recalibrating. Whatever you came for, Kenny Dixon Jr. won't hand it over on your schedule. Born in Los Angeles and raised in Detroit, he has worked this way for three decades, and the method hasn't moved. It starts with records. He worked at Detroit's Buy-Rite Music before starting his own labels. When he launched KDJ Records in 1994, he released only 12-inch singles and EPs on it. He named one 2007 track "Technologystolemyvinyle", and in 2010 he was still telling a Red Bull Music Academy audience, "I sell vinyl." The city that kept him Melbourne took a while to get him, then kept him. He made a rare visit in April 2012 and came back for Golden Plains in March 2013, on a bill with George Clinton and Parliament Funkadelic and Mulatu Astatke. On Melbourne Cup Eve in 2022 he and Omar S headlined a warehouse party at The Thorn. Last year he played Northcote Theatre twice: in February on a shared bill with Carl Craig and Marcel Dettmann, and in November on his own, to a sold-out room. A city of record shops, community radio and long sets was always going to trust the person holding the records. "I keep Detroit dust under my feet no matter where I'm standing," he said in 2019. Or, as he told Resident Advisor: "I'm coming to bring Detroit to your stage." Melbourne has never been sold an export version of Moodymann, and it keeps asking for more. This November On Saturday 28 November he plays the main stage at CORE Melbourne, as Tomorrowland's CORE brand makes its Australian debut at The Nursery, Flemington Racecourse, on a bill that also includes TSHA and Honey Dijon. It sold out in August. For everyone who missed out, there's Sunday: Moodymann plays Forum Melbourne on 29 November, with special guest TSHA.

d: Twenty years after a Kyoto lab found a way to reset a cell’s clock, the idea has reached its first human patients. Now comes the hard part: proving it works.
x: The treatment arrives the way many eye medicines do, through a fine needle into the eye. What is different is the cargo: three genes that, for the first time in a human being, are meant to make old cells behave as if they were young again. In June, Boston company Life Biosciences dosed the first patient with the therapy, ER-100, in a small safety trial for glaucoma and NAION, a cause of sudden vision loss. It is the first time partial epigenetic reprogramming, one of longevity science's most hyped ideas, has left the animal lab. A reset button in Kyoto The idea began with Shinya Yamanaka. In 2006 his lab at Kyoto University showed that switching on four genes could turn an adult mouse cell back into an embryonic-like stem cell. A year later his team did the same with human skin cells, work that earned him a share of the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The Yamanaka factors work almost too well. Left on in a living animal, they wipe a cell's identity and can trigger tumours. So researchers tried a gentler version: switch the factors on briefly, or use only some of them, so cells shed the chemical marks of age without forgetting their jobs. Harvard geneticist David Sinclair became the idea's loudest champion. In 2020 his lab reported that three of the factors, known as OSK, reversed vision loss in mice with a glaucoma-like condition and in old mice, and helped injured optic nerves regrow. A clean result would mean a reset button found in a Kyoto lab two decades ago had finally been pressed in a person. From mice to people ER-100 pairs those three genes with a safety switch. They turn on only while a patient takes the antibiotic doxycycline, for about eight weeks, and only in one eye. Up to 18 people are due to take part, at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, Columbia University's Harkness Eye Institute in New York, a clinic in Glendale, California and the Charleston Neuroscience Institute in South Carolina. Starting with the eye is deliberate. Before dosing began, Daniel Ives, chief executive of the rejuvenation startup Shift Bioscience, put it plainly to MIT Technology Review: "If it goes wrong, you've still got one left." Sinclair, a co-founder of Life Biosciences, called the trial "the first opportunity to test whether restoring that information can ameliorate human disease." His ambitions reach well beyond eyesight. In January he posted on X that "aging has a relatively simple explanation and is apparently reversible." He plans to enter an oral reprogramming drug, code-named SL-100, in the $101 million XPrize Healthspan competition. "What we're aiming to do is to epigenetically restore the animal and eventually the person," he said. The doubters Not everyone is cheering. Pete Williams, a neurobiologist at the Centre for Eye Research Australia, fears a failure could set back the whole field: "If this goes catastrophically wrong, it might screw us all in the future." The doxycycline switch, built from parts of E. coli and herpes virus genes, has never been tried in humans, so an immune reaction is possible. Sinclair's animal data on his oral drugs is unpublished, and another Harvard team found that its own chemical cocktail either did nothing in mice or was toxic. Critics also cite his record: in 2024 he stepped down as president of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research after claiming a supplement had reversed ageing in dogs. The first answers The first data came sooner than expected. On 8 October, Life Biosciences reported that the first three glaucoma patients had tolerated ER-100 through day 56, that two of the three had improved visual fields, and that the trial's safety board had recommended moving to a higher dose. Three patients in a safety study cannot show that a treatment works, and the trial was not designed to. Its estimated primary completion date is May 2027.
